g6-patterns.title: Patterns in Mathematics
g6-patterns.subtitle: Number sequences, pictures of numbers, and shape sequences

sheet.title: Important number sequences
items: Counting numbers: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \dots$
Odd numbers: $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, \dots$
Even numbers: $2, 4, 6, 8, 10, \dots$
Triangular numbers: $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \dots$
Square numbers: $1, 4, 9, 16, 25, \dots$
Cube numbers: $1, 8, 27, 64, 125, \dots$
Virahānka numbers: $1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \dots$
Powers of 2: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, \dots$ and powers of 3: $1, 3, 9, 27, 81, \dots$

sheet.title: Links between sequences
items: $1+3+5+\dots$ (first $n$ odd numbers) $=n\times n$
$1+2+\dots+n+\dots+2+1=n\times n$
Two triangular numbers next to each other add to a square: $6+10=16$
$1+2+4+\dots+(\text{a power of }2)+1=$ the next power of 2

sheet.title: Shape sequences
items: Regular polygons: $3, 4, 5, 6, \dots$ sides
Lines joining every pair of dots: $0, 1, 3, 6, 10, \dots$ (triangular numbers)
Koch snowflake: sides are multiplied by 4 at every step: $3, 12, 48, \dots$

lessons.title: Number sequences and their rules
lessons.introduction: A sequence is a list of numbers in a fixed order. To continue a sequence, look at how each number comes from the one before it. Then test your rule on every term.
formulas: Look at the difference between neighbouring terms
In the Virahānka sequence, each term is the sum of the two terms before it

picture.caption: Each row follows one rule. Read across to see the rule.

examples.question: Write the next three terms: $5, 11, 17, 23, \dots$
steps: The difference between neighbouring terms is $6$.

examples.question: Write the next two terms: $3, 6, 12, 24, \dots$
steps: Each term is double the term before it.

examples.question: Write the next two Virahānka numbers after $1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13$.
steps: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it.

lessons.title: Picturing numbers with dots
lessons.introduction: Some numbers make neat shapes when we draw them as dots. Triangular numbers make triangles. Square numbers make squares. A picture often shows why a pattern is true.
formulas: Two triangular numbers next to each other make a square

picture.caption: Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10 and square numbers 1, 4, 9 drawn as dots.

examples.question: Find the 6th triangular number.
steps: Add the first six counting numbers.

examples.question: Find the 7th square number.
steps: A square with 7 rows of 7 dots.

examples.question: Show that the 4th and 5th triangular numbers make the 5th square number.

lessons.title: Adding odd numbers
lessons.introduction: Start with one square tile. Add an L-shape of 3 tiles, then 5 tiles, then 7 tiles. Each time you get a bigger square. So the sum of the first few odd numbers is always a square number.
formulas: Sum of the first $n$ odd numbers $=n\times n$

picture.caption: Each colour is one odd number of tiles: 1 (coral), 3 (sky), 5 (green), 7 (purple). Together they make a 4 × 4 square.

examples.question: Find $1+3+5+7+9$ without adding one by one.
steps: These are the first 5 odd numbers.

examples.question: Find the sum of the first 10 odd numbers.
How many odd numbers, starting from 1, add up to 64? What is the last one?

lessons.title: Counting up and down
lessons.introduction: Count up from 1 to a number and then back down to 1. Add all the numbers. The answer is always a square number. The picture shows the numbers as columns of a staircase that fits into a square.

examples.question: An up-and-down sum is $81$. What is its top number?

lessons.title: Powers of 2 and powers of 3
lessons.introduction: Fold a sheet of paper in half again and again. The number of layers doubles each time: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16$. These are the powers of 2. If we add the powers of 2 and then add 1, we get the next power of 2.
formulas: Powers of 2: each term is $2\times$ the term before

picture.caption: Layers of paper after 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 folds: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.

examples.question: Find $1+2+4+8+16+32$ quickly.
steps: Add 1: the sum becomes the next power of 2.
The next power of 2 after 32 is 64.

examples.question: How many layers do you get after folding a paper 6 times?
Check the rule $2\times(1+3+9+27)+1=81$.

lessons.title: Shape sequences
lessons.introduction: Shapes can also form sequences. Put dots on a circle and join every pair of dots. The number of lines gives the triangular numbers again. In the Koch snowflake, every side is replaced by 4 smaller sides at each step.

picture.caption: Joining every pair of dots: 3 dots give 3 lines, 4 dots give 6 lines, 5 dots give 10 lines.

examples.question: How many lines join every pair of 6 dots?
steps: Each new dot joins all the old dots.

examples.question: The Koch snowflake has 3, 12, 48 sides. Find the number of sides at the next step.
steps: Each step multiplies the number of sides by 4.

examples.question: Stacked squares: 1 square, then a 2 by 2 stack, then a 3 by 3 stack. How many small squares are in the 8th shape?
steps: The $n$th shape is an $n$ by $n$ square.

g6-lines-angles.title: Lines and Angles
g6-lines-angles.subtitle: Points, lines, rays, angles, turning, and measuring with a protractor

sheet.title: Basic figures
items: Point: an exact position, named with a capital letter
Line segment $\overline{AB}$: the shortest path from $A$ to $B$; it has two end points
Line $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$: goes on forever in both directions
Ray $\overrightarrow{OA}$: starts at $O$ and goes on forever through $A$

sheet.title: Angles
items: An angle is made by two rays with a common start point (the vertex)
$\angle ABC$: vertex $B$, arms $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$
Full turn $=360^\circ$, half turn $=180^\circ$, quarter turn $=90^\circ$

sheet.title: Types of angles
items: Acute: less than $90^\circ$
Right: exactly $90^\circ$
Obtuse: between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$
Straight: exactly $180^\circ$
Reflex: between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$

lessons.title: Points, line segments, lines and rays
lessons.introduction: A point shows an exact place. A line segment joins two points and stops at both. A line goes on forever in both directions. A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction.
formulas: Symbols: segment $\overline{AB}$ (a bar, no arrows), line $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ (arrows at both ends), ray $\overrightarrow{AB}$ (one arrow, pointing away from the start point $A$)
Through two points there is exactly one line
A segment has 2 end points, a ray has 1, a line has none
Ray $\overrightarrow{OA}$ starts at $O$: the first letter is the start point

$\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BA}$ are the same segment, $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overleftrightarrow{BA}$ are the same line, but $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BA}$ are different rays

items.v: ray OX: starts at O and goes on forever

picture.caption: A point, a line segment, a line with arrows at both ends, and a ray with one arrow.

examples.question: Name all the line segments in triangle $ABC$.
How many line segments can you draw with 4 points, when no three of them are on one line?
steps: Each pair of points gives one segment.

examples.question: Are $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{QP}$ the same?
Write in symbols: (i) the line segment joining $X$ and $Y$; (ii) the ray that starts at $M$ and passes through $N$; (iii) the line through $P$ and $Q$.
steps: A segment has a bar over the letters.
A ray has one arrow. The start point is written first.
A line has arrows at both ends.

examples.question: Is $\overline{AB}=\overline{BA}$? Is $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{BA}$?
steps: A segment has no direction: both names give the same two end points.
A ray has a start point. $\overrightarrow{AB}$ starts at $A$, but $\overrightarrow{BA}$ starts at $B$.
examples.result: Yes for the segment, no for the rays

lessons.title: What is an angle?
lessons.introduction: Two rays that start at the same point make an angle. The common point is the vertex. The rays are the arms. We write the vertex letter in the middle when we name an angle.
formulas: $\angle ABC$ and $\angle CBA$ are the same angle

picture.caption: Angle ABC: vertex B, arms BA and BC.

examples.question: Name the vertex and the arms of $\angle PQR$.
steps: The middle letter is the vertex.

examples.question: Three rays $\overrightarrow{OA}$, $\overrightarrow{OB}$, $\overrightarrow{OC}$ start at $O$. How many angles do they make?
steps: Each pair of rays makes one angle.

examples.question: The hands of a clock show 3 o’clock. Which point is the vertex of the angle between the hands?
steps: Both hands start at the centre of the clock.

lessons.title: Turning and degrees
lessons.introduction: An angle tells us how much we turn. One full turn is divided into 360 equal parts called degrees. A half turn is 180 degrees and a quarter turn is 90 degrees.
formulas: The minute hand turns $6^\circ$ every minute

items.v: quarter turn = 90° · half turn = 180° · full turn = 360°

picture.caption: A full turn is 360°. The shaded quarter is 90°.

examples.question: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 15 minutes?
steps: 60 minutes make a full turn of $360^\circ$.
15 minutes is a quarter of an hour.

examples.question: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 20 minutes?
You face north and turn clockwise to face west. How much do you turn?
steps: North to east, east to south, south to west: 3 quarter turns.

lessons.title: Measuring angles with a protractor
lessons.introduction: A protractor has two scales from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$. Put its centre on the vertex. Put the base line on one arm. Read the scale that starts at $0^\circ$ on that arm.
formulas: Centre of the protractor on the vertex
Read the scale that starts from $0^\circ$
The two scales at a mark always add to $180^\circ$

items.v: centre on the vertex · base line on one arm

picture.caption: Measuring a 60° angle with a protractor.

examples.question: One scale reads $50^\circ$ at a mark. What does the other scale read at the same mark?
Find the angle between the hands of a clock at 4 o’clock.
steps: The 12 numbers divide $360^\circ$: each gap is $30^\circ$.

examples.question: Find the angle between the hands of a clock at 6 o’clock.
steps: From 12 to 6 there are 6 gaps of $30^\circ$.

lessons.title: Types of angles
lessons.introduction: We sort angles by size. An angle smaller than a right angle is acute. An angle between a right angle and a straight angle is obtuse. An angle bigger than a straight angle is reflex.

picture.caption: Acute, right, obtuse and straight angles.

examples.question: Sort these angles: $35^\circ, 90^\circ, 145^\circ, 180^\circ, 250^\circ$.
What type of angle do the clock hands make at 2 o’clock?
An angle is $70^\circ$. What is the reflex angle on the other side of its arms?
steps: Together they make a full turn.

lessons.title: Angles on a line and around a point
lessons.introduction: A ray that stands on a straight line splits the straight angle into two angles. These two angles add to $180^\circ$. All the angles around one point add to $360^\circ$.
formulas: Angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$
Angles around a point add to $360^\circ$

picture.caption: The two angles on the straight line add to 180°.

examples.question: Two angles on a straight line are $x$ and $65^\circ$. Find $x$.
Three angles around a point are $100^\circ$, $140^\circ$ and $y$. Find $y$.
A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices from the centre. Find the angle of each slice.
steps: The angles around the centre add to $360^\circ$.

g6-number-play.title: Number Play
g6-number-play.subtitle: Parity, supercells, magic squares, palindromes, Kaprekar’s number and the Collatz conjecture

sheet.title: Parity (odd and even)
items: even $+$ even $=$ even
odd $+$ odd $=$ even
odd $+$ even $=$ odd
A sum of an odd number of odd numbers is odd
odd $\times$ odd $=$ odd; any number $\times$ even $=$ even

sheet.title: Magic squares
items: Every row, column and diagonal has the same sum (the magic sum)
With $1$ to $9$: magic sum $=\frac{1+2+\dots+9}{3}=\frac{45}{3}=15$
The centre of a $3\times3$ magic square with $1$ to $9$ is $5$

sheet.title: Digit games
items: Palindrome: reads the same both ways, like $121$ or $4334$
Reverse-and-add often leads to a palindrome
Kaprekar: largest minus smallest arrangement of 4 digits reaches $6174$
Collatz: if even, halve; if odd, $3\times$ the number $+1$; the sequence seems to reach $1$ always

lessons.title: Numbers can tell a story: supercells
lessons.introduction: In a row of numbers, a supercell is a number that is bigger than each of its neighbours. To find supercells, compare every number with the number on its left and the number on its right.
formulas: Compare each number with all its neighbours
An end cell has only one neighbour
Two neighbours can never both be supercells

picture.caption: The gold cells 43, 75 and 61 are bigger than both their neighbours.

examples.question: Find the supercells in the row $26, 43, 18, 75, 32, 61, 59, 12$.
steps: The others are smaller than a neighbour.

examples.question: A row has 6 cells. What is the largest number of supercells it can have?
steps: Two neighbours cannot both be supercells.
So at most every second cell: cells 1, 3, 5 or cells 2, 4, 6.

examples.question: Make a row of 5 different numbers with no supercell in the middle three cells.
steps: Each middle number is smaller than its right neighbour.
Only the last cell, $5$, is a supercell.

lessons.title: Picking parity
lessons.introduction: Every whole number is odd or even. This is its parity. We can often find the parity of an answer without working out the answer. Pair up the odd numbers: each pair makes an even sum.
formulas: An odd count of odd numbers adds to an odd number

picture.caption: Parity table for addition: odd + odd = even.

examples.question: Is $23+45+67$ odd or even?
steps: It is a sum of three odd numbers.
Three is an odd count, so the sum is odd.

examples.question: Can 5 odd numbers add up to $30$?
steps: A sum of 5 odd numbers is odd.

examples.question: Is $7\times8+5$ odd or even?
steps: $7\times8$ is even (it has an even factor).

lessons.title: Magic squares
lessons.introduction: In a magic square, every row, every column and both diagonals add to the same number. With the numbers 1 to 9, the total is 45. The three rows share this total, so each row adds to 15.
formulas: Magic sum $=$ total $\div$ number of rows
The centre is the middle number, $5$
Adding the same number to every cell gives a new magic square

picture.caption: Every row, column and diagonal adds to 15. The centre is 5.

examples.question: Find the magic sum of a $3\times3$ magic square that uses $1$ to $9$.
Make a magic square with the numbers $2$ to $10$.
steps: Add $1$ to every number in the square $4, 9, 2 \,|\, 3, 5, 7 \,|\, 8, 1, 6$.

examples.question: A magic square uses $1$ to $9$. Its top row is $8, 1, ?$. Find the missing number.

lessons.title: Palindromes and reverse-and-add
lessons.introduction: A palindrome reads the same from left to right and from right to left, like 121. Take a number, reverse its digits and add. Repeat. Very often you reach a palindrome.

picture.caption: Reverse-and-add from 68 reaches the palindrome 1111 in three steps.

examples.question: Use reverse-and-add on $68$ until you get a palindrome.
How many three-digit palindromes are there?
steps: The first digit can be $1$ to $9$: 9 ways.
The middle digit can be $0$ to $9$: 10 ways.
The last digit must equal the first.

examples.question: Find the digit sum of $4568$.

lessons.title: Kaprekar’s magic number 6174
lessons.introduction: Take a 4-digit number whose digits are not all the same. Arrange its digits from largest to smallest, and from smallest to largest. Subtract. Repeat with the answer. You always reach 6174 in at most 7 steps.
formulas: Keep zeros: $0378$ counts as a 4-digit arrangement
For 3-digit numbers the end number is $495$

picture.caption: Kaprekar’s routine on 3524 reaches 6174.

examples.question: Apply Kaprekar’s routine to $3524$.
Apply Kaprekar’s routine to $2026$.
Apply the 3-digit routine to $352$.

lessons.title: The Collatz conjecture
lessons.introduction: Start with any whole number. If it is even, halve it. If it is odd, multiply it by 3 and add 1. Mathematicians think that you always reach 1, but nobody has proved it yet. This open question is the Collatz conjecture.
formulas: Every number tested so far reaches $1$

items.v: sky: even, so halve it · coral: odd, so 3 × number + 1 · green: the end

picture.caption: The Collatz sequence of 6 reaches 1.

examples.question: Write the Collatz sequence that starts at $6$.
How many steps does the Collatz sequence of $7$ take to reach $1$?
Which number comes just before $16$ in a Collatz sequence, if that number is odd?

g6-data.title: Data Handling and Presentation
g6-data.subtitle: Collecting data, tally marks, pictographs and bar graphs

sheet.title: Organising data
items: Data: facts and numbers collected for a purpose
Tally marks: one stroke for each item; every fifth stroke crosses four
Frequency: how many times an item appears

sheet.title: Pictographs
items: A picture stands for a fixed number of items (the key)
A half picture stands for half that number
Number of items $=$ number of pictures $\times$ value of one picture

sheet.title: Bar graphs
items: Bars of equal width with equal gaps
Height of a bar shows the frequency
Scale: for example $1$ unit $=10$ items
Bar height $=$ value $\div$ scale value

lessons.title: Collecting and organising data
lessons.introduction: When we collect data, the numbers are often mixed up. A table with tally marks puts them in order. Draw one stroke for each item. Every fifth stroke goes across the four before it, so we can count in fives.
formulas: Total of the frequencies $=$ total number of items

picture.caption: Favourite fruits of 30 students, with tally marks.

examples.question: How many items do the tally marks 卌 卌 ||| show?
Use the table of favourite fruits. How many students chose mango or banana?
Use the table of favourite fruits. How many students are there in all?

lessons.title: Pictographs
lessons.introduction: A pictograph shows data with pictures. The key tells us how many items one picture stands for. A half picture stands for half of that number.
formulas: Value $=$ number of pictures $\times$ value of one picture
Half a picture $=$ half the value

picture.caption: A pictograph of favourite games. One circle stands for 10 students.

examples.question: In the pictograph, Football has two and a half circles. How many students chose football?
How many more students chose cricket than chess?
One picture stands for 10 students. How do you show 35 students?
steps: Draw 3 full pictures and one half picture.

lessons.title: Reading bar graphs
lessons.introduction: In a bar graph, each bar stands for one item. All bars have the same width. The height of a bar shows how many. Read the value at the top of each bar, then compare.
formulas: The tallest bar shows the greatest value
Total $=$ sum of all the values

picture.caption: Number of samosas sold at a school canteen in one week.

examples.question: On which day were the most samosas sold?
How many more samosas were sold on Tuesday than on Wednesday?
How many samosas were sold in the whole week?

lessons.title: Drawing a bar graph with a scale
lessons.introduction: When the numbers are large, we use a scale. For example, 1 unit of height stands for 50 books. Divide each value by 50 to get the height of its bar.
formulas: Choose a scale that keeps the bars a good size
Label both axes and write the scale

picture.caption: Library books read by each class. Scale: 1 unit = 50 books.

examples.question: With the scale $1$ unit $=50$ books, how tall is the bar for Class 7?
A bar is $3$ units tall. How many books does it show?
The values are $120, 260, 210, 90$. Is $1$ unit $=10$ or $1$ unit $=20$ the better scale for a page with room for 15 units?
steps: With $1$ unit $=10$: the tallest bar is $26$ units, too tall.
With $1$ unit $=20$: the tallest bar is $13$ units, which fits.

lessons.title: Comparing data and drawing conclusions
lessons.introduction: Graphs help us answer questions quickly. We can find the most and the least, compare two items, and see changes. Always read the scale before you compare.
formulas: Most and least: tallest and shortest bars
How many times: divide the two values
Check that the scale starts at $0$

picture.caption: Rainfall in millimetres in four months.

examples.question: Which month had the least rain?
steps: The shortest bar is September, $90$ mm.

examples.question: How much more rain fell in July than in June?
Find the total rainfall in the four months.

lessons.title: Missing values and careful reading
lessons.introduction: Sometimes one value is missing, but we know the total. Subtract the known values from the total. Also check whether a graph starts at zero. A graph that does not start at zero can make small differences look big.
formulas: A broken scale can mislead the reader
Write the scale and the title on every graph

picture.caption: Colours chosen by 36 students. The yellow bar was found from the total.

examples.question: 36 students chose a colour. Red $12$, blue $9$, green $7$. How many chose yellow?
A graph starts at $100$, not at $0$. One bar shows $110$ and the other shows $120$. The second bar looks twice as tall. Is $120$ twice $110$?
steps: But $120$ is not twice $110$; it is only $10$ more.

examples.question: In a pictograph, 1 picture $=4$ books. The total is $40$ books. The rows that are drawn show $28$ books. How many pictures does the missing row need?

g6-prime-time.title: Prime Time
g6-prime-time.subtitle: Common multiples and factors, primes, co-primes, prime factorisation and divisibility tests

sheet.title: Multiples and factors
items: A multiple of $a$: $a, 2a, 3a, \dots$
A factor of $n$ divides $n$ with no remainder
Common multiple: a multiple of both numbers
Common factor: a factor of both numbers

sheet.title: Primes
items: Prime: exactly two factors, $1$ and itself: $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, \dots$
Composite: more than two factors
$1$ is neither prime nor composite
Co-prime numbers: their only common factor is $1$

sheet.title: Divisibility tests
items: By $2$: last digit $0, 2, 4, 6, 8$
By $4$: the last two digits make a multiple of $4$
By $5$: last digit $0$ or $5$
By $8$: the last three digits make a multiple of $8$
By $10$: last digit $0$
By $3$ (or $9$): the digit sum is a multiple of $3$ (or $9$)

lessons.title: Common multiples and common factors
lessons.introduction: In the idli–vada game, children count in turn. On a multiple of 3 they say “idli”, and on a multiple of 5 they say “vada”. On a multiple of both they say “idli–vada”. These numbers are the common multiples of 3 and 5.

picture.caption: Multiples of 3 up to 30. The gold points 15 and 30 are also multiples of 5.

examples.question: When does a child first say “idli–vada”, for multiples of 3 and 5?
steps: The first common multiple of $3$ and $5$ is $15$.

examples.question: List the common multiples of $4$ and $6$ below $50$.
Find all the factors of $36$.

lessons.title: Prime and composite numbers
lessons.introduction: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two factors. To find primes, cross out the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and so on. The numbers that stay are primes. This method is the sieve of Eratosthenes.
formulas: To test $n$, try dividing by the primes up to about $\sqrt{n}$

picture.caption: The numbers 1 to 30. The 10 primes are gold.

examples.question: How many primes are there from $1$ to $30$?
Is $91$ prime?
Twin primes differ by 2, like $11$ and $13$. List the twin primes below $50$.

lessons.title: Co-prime numbers
lessons.introduction: Two numbers are co-prime when their only common factor is 1. They do not need to be prime themselves. For example, 8 and 15 are both composite, but they share no factor other than 1.
formulas: Two different primes are always co-prime
Two numbers next to each other, like $20$ and $21$, are co-prime

picture.caption: Co-prime numbers share only the factor 1.

examples.question: Are $15$ and $28$ co-prime?
Are $18$ and $35$ co-prime?
Are $21$ and $49$ co-prime?

lessons.title: Prime factorisation
lessons.introduction: Every composite number can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, if we ignore the order. Split the number into two factors. Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime. This picture is a factor tree.
formulas: Keep splitting until every factor is prime
The prime factors are the same, whichever split you start with

picture.caption: Factor tree: 60 = 6 × 10 = 2 × 3 × 2 × 5. Green circles are primes.

examples.question: Find the prime factorisation of $84$.
Find the prime factorisation of $360$.
Use prime factors to check whether $45$ and $56$ are co-prime.

lessons.title: Divisibility tests
lessons.introduction: A divisibility test tells us whether a number divides another, without long division. For 2, 5 and 10, look at the last digit. For 4, look at the last two digits. For 8, look at the last three digits.

picture.caption: Each example passes its test.

examples.question: Is $5124$ divisible by $4$? Is it divisible by $8$?
steps: Last two digits: $24=4\times6$, so yes for $4$.
Last three digits: $124=8\times15+4$, so no for $8$.

examples.question: Is $9480$ divisible by $8$, $5$ and $10$?
Find the digit that goes in the blank so that $34\_6$ is divisible by $3$, using the smallest digit.
steps: The next multiple of $3$ after $13$ is $15$.

lessons.title: Puzzles with primes and multiples
lessons.introduction: Many puzzles use common multiples. The smallest number that is a multiple of several numbers is their lowest common multiple. Find it from the prime factors: take each prime the greatest number of times it appears.
formulas: Lowest common multiple (LCM) of $4$ and $6$ is $12$
Use the prime factors to find the LCM

picture.caption: Bell A rings every 6 minutes and bell B every 9 minutes. They ring together at 18 and 36.

examples.question: Two bells ring every 6 minutes and every 9 minutes. They ring together now. After how many minutes do they ring together again?
Find the smallest number that is divisible by every number from $1$ to $10$.
I am a two-digit prime. My digits add to $10$, and I am less than $30$. Who am I?
steps: Two-digit numbers below 30 with digit sum 10: $19$ and $28$.
$28$ is even, so it is not prime. $19$ is prime.

g6-perimeter-area.title: Perimeter and Area
g6-perimeter-area.subtitle: Perimeter of shapes, area on squared paper, rectangles, squares and triangles

sheet.title: Perimeter (distance around)
items: Rectangle: $P=2\times(\text{length}+\text{breadth})$
Square: $P=4\times\text{side}$
Triangle: $P=$ sum of the three sides
Regular polygon with $n$ sides: $P=n\times\text{side}$

sheet.title: Area (space covered)
items: Area is counted in square units: $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$
Rectangle: $A=\text{length}\times\text{breadth}$
Square: $A=\text{side}\times\text{side}$
Triangle: $A=\frac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$

sheet.title: Squared paper
items: Count full squares
Two half squares make one square
More than half: count as 1; less than half: leave out (for estimates)

lessons.title: Perimeter
lessons.introduction: Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a shape. Imagine walking once around a park: the distance you walk is its perimeter. Add the lengths of all the sides.

picture.caption: Perimeter: add all the sides.

examples.question: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length $8$ cm and breadth $5$ cm.
A regular hexagon has sides of $7$ cm. Find its perimeter.
A square field has a perimeter of $96$ m. Find the length of one side.

lessons.title: Area of rectangles and squares
lessons.introduction: Area tells us how much flat space a shape covers. We count how many unit squares fit inside it. A rectangle with 4 rows of 6 unit squares has an area of $4\times6=24$ square units.

picture.caption: A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle is covered by 24 unit squares.

examples.question: Find the area of a rectangle $9$ cm long and $4$ cm wide.
Find the area of a square with side $12$ m.
A rectangle has area $60\ \text{cm}^2$ and length $12$ cm. Find its breadth.

lessons.title: Area on squared paper
lessons.introduction: For a shape drawn on squared paper, count the full squares first. Then pair up the half squares: two halves make one whole square. Add the two counts.
formulas: Total area $=$ full squares $+$ half the number of half squares

items.v: 16 full squares + 4 half squares = 18 square units

picture.caption: A shape on squared paper: sky squares are full squares, orange triangles are half squares.

examples.question: A shape covers $16$ full squares and $4$ half squares. Find its area.
A shape covers $10$ full squares and $6$ half squares. Find its area.
Each square on the paper is $1$ cm by $1$ cm. A leaf covers about $23$ squares. What is its area?

lessons.title: Area of a triangle
lessons.introduction: Draw a triangle inside a rectangle so that its base is the bottom of the rectangle and its top corner touches the top side. The triangle covers exactly half of the rectangle.
formulas: The height is perpendicular to the base
A diagonal cuts a rectangle into two equal triangles

items.v: The triangle fills half of the rectangle

picture.caption: The triangle covers half of the 10 cm by 6 cm rectangle.

examples.question: Find the area of the triangle in the picture: base $10$ cm, height $6$ cm.
A right-angled triangle has the two shorter sides $6$ cm and $8$ cm. Find its area.
steps: The two shorter sides are the base and the height.

examples.question: A square of side $10$ cm is cut along a diagonal. Find the area of one triangle.

lessons.title: Same perimeter, different areas
lessons.introduction: Shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas. With a 20 cm string, we can make many rectangles. The closer the rectangle is to a square, the bigger its area.
formulas: Same perimeter does not mean same area
For a fixed perimeter, the square has the greatest area
Same area can also have different perimeters

picture.caption: Rectangles with perimeter 20 cm. The square 5 cm by 5 cm has the greatest area.

examples.question: List rectangles with whole-number sides and perimeter $20$ cm. Which one has the greatest area?
Two rectangles have area $36\ \text{cm}^2$: $4\times9$ and $6\times6$. Find their perimeters.
A $12$ by $1$ rectangle and a $4$ by $3$ rectangle have the same area. Which has the longer perimeter?

lessons.title: Shapes made of rectangles
lessons.introduction: Split a complex shape into rectangles. Find the area of each part and add. For the perimeter, walk around the outside only. Do not count the line that you drew to split the shape.
formulas: Area: split into rectangles and add
Perimeter: add the outer sides only
Find a missing side from the opposite sides

picture.caption: An L-shaped garden split into rectangles A and B.

examples.question: Find the area of the L-shaped garden.
Find the perimeter of the L-shaped garden.
A path $1$ m wide goes around the outside of a $10$ m by $6$ m lawn. Find the area of the path.

g6-fractions.title: Fractions
g6-fractions.subtitle: Fractional units, the number line, mixed fractions, equivalent fractions, comparing, adding and subtracting

sheet.title: Meaning
items: $\frac{a}{b}$: $a$ parts out of $b$ equal parts
Fractional unit: $\frac1b$ (one of $b$ equal parts)
Numerator: top number; denominator: bottom number

sheet.title: Equivalent fractions
items: Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number: $\frac12=\frac24=\frac36$
Simplest form: top and bottom have no common factor except $1$

sheet.title: Mixed fractions
items: $\frac{17}{5}=3\frac25$ (divide: $17=3\times5+2$)

sheet.title: Compare, add and subtract
items: Same denominator: compare or add the numerators
Different denominators: first change to a common denominator

lessons.title: Fractional units
lessons.introduction: When one whole is cut into equal parts, each part is a fractional unit. Cut a roti into 3 equal parts: each part is one-third, $\frac13$. More parts means smaller parts.

picture.caption: The same whole cut into 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 equal parts. One part is shaded in each row.

examples.question: Which is bigger, $\frac15$ or $\frac18$?
steps: The whole is cut into fewer parts for $\frac15$.

examples.question: How many $\frac14$ pieces make $3$ wholes?
A ribbon of $1$ m is cut into $5$ equal pieces. How long is each piece?
steps: Each piece is $\frac15$ of the ribbon.

lessons.title: Fractions on the number line and mixed fractions
lessons.introduction: To mark $\frac74$ on a number line, cut each unit into 4 equal parts. Count 7 parts from 0. We pass 1 whole and 3 more quarters, so $\frac74=1\frac34$.
formulas: Cut each unit into $b$ equal parts to mark $\frac ab$
Improper to mixed: divide the numerator by the denominator
Mixed to improper: whole $\times$ denominator $+$ numerator

picture.caption: Each unit is cut into quarters. 7/4 = 1 3/4 is 3 quarters past 1.

examples.question: Write $\frac{17}{5}$ as a mixed fraction.
Write $2\frac34$ as an improper fraction.
Between which two whole numbers does $\frac{23}{6}$ lie?

lessons.title: Equivalent fractions and simplest form
lessons.introduction: Half a chocolate bar is the same amount as two quarters or four eighths. These fractions are equivalent. Multiply or divide the top and the bottom by the same number to get an equivalent fraction.
formulas: Simplest form: divide top and bottom by their highest common factor

picture.caption: 1/2, 2/4 and 4/8 cover the same length: they are equivalent.

examples.question: Write two fractions equivalent to $\frac35$.
Write $\frac{18}{24}$ in its simplest form.
steps: The highest common factor of $18$ and $24$ is $6$.

examples.question: Find the missing number: $\frac{3}{4}=\frac{\square}{20}$.
steps: $4\times5=20$, so multiply the top by $5$ too.

lessons.title: Comparing fractions
lessons.introduction: With the same denominator, the fraction with the bigger numerator is bigger. With different denominators, first change both fractions to a common denominator. Then compare the numerators.
formulas: Same numerator: the smaller denominator is bigger

examples.question: Which is bigger, $\frac34$ or $\frac23$?
Which is bigger, $\frac56$ or $\frac79$?
Arrange in increasing order: $\frac12, \frac38, \frac34$.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
lessons.introduction: We can add quarters to quarters, just like apples to apples. With the same denominator, add or subtract the numerators. With different denominators, first change them to a common denominator.
formulas: Different denominators: use the lowest common multiple

examples.question: Find $\frac14+\frac24$.
Find $\frac23+\frac14$.
Meena had $\frac56$ of a cake. She gave $\frac14$ of the cake to Ravi. How much is left?

lessons.title: Unit fractions and Brahmagupta’s method
lessons.introduction: Ancient Egyptians wrote fractions as sums of different unit fractions, like $\frac34=\frac12+\frac14$. The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta gave the rule for adding fractions: make the denominators equal, then add the numerators.

picture.caption: Adding 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16: the shaded part grows closer to the whole.

examples.question: Check that $\frac12=\frac13+\frac16$.
Find $\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\frac1{16}$.
Write $\frac56$ as a sum of two different unit fractions.

g6-constructions.title: Playing with Constructions
g6-constructions.subtitle: Circles with a compass, rectangles and squares, diagonals and equal distances

sheet.title: Circles
items: Centre: the fixed middle point
Radius: distance from the centre to the circle
Diameter $=2\times$ radius; it passes through the centre
All points of a circle are at the same distance from the centre

sheet.title: Rectangles and squares
items: Opposite sides are equal; all angles are $90^\circ$
The diagonals are equal and cut each other in half
A square has all four sides equal
The diagonals of a square also meet at $90^\circ$

sheet.title: Equal distances
items: Points at equal distance from $A$ and $B$ lie on one line
This line passes through the mid-point of $AB$ at $90^\circ$
Find it with two arcs of the same radius from $A$ and $B$

lessons.title: Circles and the compass
lessons.introduction: A compass draws a circle. Fix its point at the centre and turn the pencil around. The pencil stays at the same distance from the centre. This distance is the radius.
formulas: Set the compass to the radius before you draw

picture.caption: A circle with its centre, a radius and a diameter, drawn with a compass.

examples.question: A circle has radius $4$ cm. Find its diameter.
A circular plate has diameter $26$ cm. Find its radius.
How wide must you open a compass to draw a circle with diameter $10$ cm?
steps: The compass opening is the radius.

lessons.title: Points at a given distance
lessons.introduction: All the points that are 3 cm from a point O form a circle with centre O and radius 3 cm. Points closer to O are inside the circle. Points farther away are outside.

items.v: every point on the circle is 3 cm from O

picture.caption: Points on, inside and outside a circle of radius 3 cm.

examples.question: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $5$ cm. Point $P$ is $3$ cm from $O$. Where is $P$?
A goat is tied to a pole with a rope $7$ m long. Describe the region where the goat can graze.
steps: The goat can reach every point up to $7$ m from the pole.
examples.result: A circular region with radius $7$ m and the pole at the centre

examples.question: Two circles with centre $O$ have radii $3$ cm and $5$ cm. How far apart are the circles, measured along a radius?

lessons.title: Rectangles and squares
lessons.introduction: A rectangle has four right angles, and its opposite sides are equal. Its two diagonals are equal and they cut each other in half. A square is a rectangle with all four sides equal.
formulas: Diagonals equal and they bisect each other
Square: all sides equal; diagonals meet at $90^\circ$

items.v: AC = BD, and they cut each other in half

picture.caption: Rectangle ABCD with its two diagonals.

examples.question: In rectangle $ABCD$, $AB=9$ cm and $BC=5$ cm. Find $CD$ and $DA$.
The diagonal $AC$ of a rectangle is $10$ cm. Find $BD$, and the distance from $A$ to the point where the diagonals meet.
steps: They cut each other in half: $10\div2=5$ cm.

examples.question: Is every square a rectangle? Is every rectangle a square?
steps: A square has all angles $90^\circ$ and opposite sides equal.
A rectangle need not have all sides equal.
examples.result: Every square is a rectangle; not every rectangle is a square

lessons.title: Constructing a rectangle
lessons.introduction: To draw a rectangle with given sides, use a ruler and a protractor (or a set square). Draw the base. Draw right angles at both ends. Mark the height on both. Join the two top points.
formulas: Step 1: draw $AB$ of the given length
Step 3: mark $AD$ and $BC$ of the given height

picture.caption: Constructing a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm.

examples.question: List the steps to construct a rectangle $6$ cm by $4$ cm.
After the construction, how can you check your rectangle?
steps: Measure both diagonals: they must be equal.
examples.result: Opposite sides and diagonals are equal

examples.question: You want a square of side $5$ cm. What changes in the steps?
steps: Mark $AD=BC=5$ cm on the right angles.

lessons.title: Points equidistant from two points
lessons.introduction: Open the compass more than half of $AB$. Draw arcs from $A$ and from $B$ with the same opening. The arcs meet at $P$ and $Q$. Every point on line $PQ$ is the same distance from $A$ and from $B$.
formulas: Arcs from $A$ and $B$ with the same radius meet at $P$ and $Q$

picture.caption: Equal arcs from A and B meet at P and Q. The red line PQ passes through the mid-point M.

examples.question: $AB=8$ cm. Where does line $PQ$ cross $AB$?
Point $P$ is on line $PQ$, and $PA=6$ cm. Find $PB$.
steps: Every point of $PQ$ is equally far from $A$ and $B$.

examples.question: Why must the compass opening be more than half of $AB$?
steps: If it is less, the two arcs do not reach each other.
examples.result: Otherwise the arcs do not meet

lessons.title: Designs with constructions
lessons.introduction: We can combine circles, squares and lines to draw designs. Plan the design first. Then construct each part with exact measures, from the biggest part to the smallest.
formulas: Mark the centres of circles before you draw them
Use the diagonals to find the centre of a square

items.v: square base · triangle roof · rectangle door · circle windows

picture.caption: A house design: a square, a triangle roof, a door and two round windows.

examples.question: How do you find the centre of a square drawing?
A square of side $6$ cm has a circle inside it that touches all four sides. Find the radius of the circle.
steps: The circle fits exactly across the square: diameter $=6$ cm.

examples.question: The roof of the house is a triangle with two sides of $5$ cm on a base of $6$ cm. Find the perimeter of the roof.

g6-symmetry.title: Symmetry
g6-symmetry.subtitle: Lines of symmetry, symmetry of quadrilaterals and their diagonals, reflection, rotational symmetry, angle and order of symmetry

sheet.title: Line symmetry
items: A line of symmetry folds a figure into two parts that match exactly
Each point and its image are equally far from the line
Square: $4$ lines; rectangle: $2$; equilateral triangle: $3$
Regular polygon with $n$ sides: $n$ lines; circle: every diameter

sheet.title: Rotational symmetry
items: A figure has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after a turn of less than $360^\circ$
Angle of symmetry: the smallest such turn
Order $=360^\circ\div$ angle of symmetry
Square: angle $90^\circ$, order $4$

sheet.title: Regular polygons
items: Equilateral triangle: angle $120^\circ$, order $3$
Regular hexagon: angle $60^\circ$, order $6$
Regular $n$-gon: angle $360^\circ\div n$

sheet.title: Quadrilaterals
items: Square: $4$ lines, order $4$; rectangle: $2$ lines, order $2$
Rhombus: $2$ lines (the diagonals), order $2$
Parallelogram: $0$ lines, order $2$
Kite: $1$ line (a diagonal); isosceles trapezium: $1$ line; no rotational symmetry

lessons.title: Line of symmetry
lessons.introduction: Fold a picture along a line. If the two halves match exactly, the line is a line of symmetry. A mirror placed on that line shows the whole picture.
formulas: The two halves match when folded
Each point and its image are at equal distance from the line
A figure can have no, one or many lines of symmetry

picture.caption: Each red dashed line is a line of symmetry.

examples.question: Which of the letters $A$, $B$, $F$, $H$, $M$ have a line of symmetry?
How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle (not a square) have?
steps: Fold across the middle, top to bottom: the halves match.
Fold across the middle, left to right: the halves match.
A fold along a diagonal does not match.

examples.question: Does the number $8$ (as a digit) have a line of symmetry?
steps: Fold along a vertical line or a horizontal line: the halves match.

examples.question: Which of these have a line of symmetry: a butterfly, a triangle with three different sides, the letter $N$?
steps: A butterfly: yes, the line along its body.
A triangle with three different sides: no fold matches.
$N$: no line of symmetry (it has a half-turn symmetry).

examples.question: Does the word $MOM$ have a standing (vertical) line of symmetry?
steps: $M$ and $O$ each have a standing line of symmetry.
The word reads the same from both ends, so its middle line works.
examples.result: Yes, through the middle of the $O$

lessons.title: Figures with many lines of symmetry
lessons.introduction: Some figures have several lines of symmetry. A regular polygon has as many lines of symmetry as sides. A circle has a line of symmetry along every diameter, so it has infinitely many.

picture.caption: A square has 4 lines of symmetry. An equilateral triangle has 3.

examples.question: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
steps: A regular polygon with $n$ sides has $n$ lines.

examples.question: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
steps: The line from the top corner to the middle of the base folds it into matching halves.

examples.question: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
steps: Every diameter folds the circle into two matching halves.

examples.question: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have?
steps: A regular polygon with $n$ sides has $n$ lines.
Each line goes through a corner and the mid-point of the opposite side.

examples.question: A shape has $4$ equal sides and $4$ lines of symmetry. Name it.
steps: A rhombus has $4$ equal sides but only $2$ lines.
Two more lines need right angles at the corners.

lessons.title: Lines of symmetry of quadrilaterals
lessons.introduction: Cut out a square, a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram, a kite and two trapeziums from paper. Fold each one in every way that you can think of. Count only the folds where the two halves fit exactly on each other. The simulation in this session lets you do the same folds on the screen.
formulas: Square: $4$ lines (two through the mid-points of opposite sides, two along the diagonals)
Rectangle: $2$ lines, through the mid-points of opposite sides
Kite: $1$ line, along the diagonal that joins the corners between the equal sides
Isosceles trapezium: $1$ line, through the mid-points of the two parallel sides
Parallelogram, and a trapezium with unequal slant sides: $0$ lines

picture.caption: Red lines are lines of symmetry. A parallelogram has none.

examples.question: How many lines of symmetry does a rhombus have? Where are they?
steps: Fold along a diagonal: the two halves fit. This is true for both diagonals.
Fold through the mid-points of opposite sides: the corners do not meet. So these are not lines of symmetry.

examples.question: A rectangle is $6$ cm long and $4$ cm wide. Describe its lines of symmetry.
steps: One standing line: $3$ cm from each short side.
One sleeping line: $2$ cm from each long side.
The diagonals are not lines of symmetry.

examples.question: Does a parallelogram (not a rectangle) have a line of symmetry?
steps: A diagonal cuts it into two equal triangles, but after a fold they do not lie on each other.
The lines through the mid-points of opposite sides also fail.

examples.question: Where is the line of symmetry of an isosceles trapezium?
steps: The two slant sides are equal.
Fold through the mid-points of the two parallel sides: the halves fit.
examples.result: $1$ line, through the mid-points of the parallel sides

examples.question: Which quadrilateral has exactly one line of symmetry, and that line is a diagonal?
steps: In a kite, the two pairs of equal sides meet at two corners.
The diagonal through these two corners is the only line of symmetry.

lessons.title: Diagonals: line of symmetry or not?
lessons.introduction: A diagonal joins two opposite corners. It always cuts a quadrilateral into two triangles. But a diagonal is a line of symmetry only when the two triangles fit on each other after a fold along it. Test each diagonal: fold, and see whether one corner lands on the opposite corner.
formulas: Square: both diagonals are lines of symmetry. The diagonals are equal, cut each other into halves and meet at $90^\circ$
Rhombus: both diagonals are lines of symmetry. They cut each other into halves at $90^\circ$, but they are not equal
Rectangle: no diagonal is a line of symmetry. The diagonals are equal and cut each other into halves
Parallelogram: no diagonal is a line of symmetry. The diagonals cut each other into halves
Kite: one diagonal is a line of symmetry. The diagonals meet at $90^\circ$

items.v: fold along AC: B goes to B′, not to D
rhombus: both diagonals are lines of symmetry

picture.caption: A diagonal always cuts a quadrilateral into two triangles. They fit on each other after a fold only for some shapes.

examples.question: Is a diagonal of a rectangle (not a square) a line of symmetry?
steps: Fold the rectangle $ABCD$ along the diagonal $AC$.
$B$ goes to a point outside the rectangle. It does not land on $D$.

examples.question: Is a diagonal of a square a line of symmetry?
steps: All sides are equal and all angles are $90^\circ$, so $B$ lands exactly on $D$.

examples.question: Which quadrilaterals have a diagonal as a line of symmetry?
In a rhombus $ABCD$, the diagonal $AC$ is a line of symmetry and $\angle BAC = 35^\circ$. Find $\angle DAC$ and $\angle BAD$.
steps: Fold along $AC$: $B$ lands on $D$, so $\angle DAC = \angle BAC = 35^\circ$.

examples.question: In a kite $ABCD$, the diagonal $AC$ is the line of symmetry. $AB = 5$ cm and $CB = 8$ cm. Find $AD$ and $CD$.

lessons.title: Completing a figure by reflection
lessons.introduction: To complete a symmetric figure, reflect each corner in the line of symmetry. A corner 4 squares to the left of the line goes to 4 squares to the right of it. Then join the reflected corners.
formulas: The image is at the same distance on the other side
The line joining a point and its image is perpendicular to the mirror line
Reflect the corners, then join them

picture.caption: The sky half is reflected in the red line to give the coral half.

examples.question: A point is $3$ squares to the left of a vertical mirror line. Where is its image?
examples.result: $3$ squares to the right of the line

examples.question: A point is $2$ squares above a horizontal mirror line. Where is its image?
A point lies on the mirror line. Where is its image?
steps: Its distance from the line is $0$.

examples.question: On a grid, the mirror line is the standing line through $x = 4$. A point is at $x = 1$. Where is its image?
steps: The point is $4 - 1 = 3$ squares to the left of the mirror.
Its image is $3$ squares to the right: $4 + 3 = 7$.

examples.question: A shaded square is $5$ squares to the left of a standing mirror line and $2$ squares above the bottom. Where is its image?
steps: The left–right distance changes side: $5$ squares to the right.
The height does not change: $2$ squares above the bottom.
examples.result: $5$ squares right of the mirror, $2$ squares up

lessons.title: Making symmetric pictures: fold, cut and blot
lessons.introduction: There are three easy ways to make a symmetric picture. Fold a paper and cut a shape along the fold. When you open it, the fold is a line of symmetry. Or put a few drops of paint on one half of a paper, fold it and press. The paint makes a mirror picture on the other half. Or fold a paper two times and cut: the open shape has two lines of symmetry.
formulas: One fold and a cut: the crease is a line of symmetry
Two folds at $90^\circ$ and a cut: both creases are lines of symmetry, and the shape has a half-turn symmetry too
Ink blot: every spot and its copy are equally far from the crease

items.v: half heart cut on a fold
open it: the fold is the line of symmetry

picture.caption: Fold, cut and open: the crease is a line of symmetry.

examples.question: You fold a paper once and cut a half heart along the fold. How many lines of symmetry does the open heart have?
steps: The two halves were cut together, so they are the same.

examples.question: You fold a paper in half, then in half again, and cut off one corner. How many lines of symmetry does the open shape have?
steps: Each crease divides the shape into two matching halves.
There are $2$ creases at $90^\circ$ to each other.

examples.question: In an ink-blot picture, a spot is $3$ cm to the left of the crease. Where is its copy?
steps: The copy is as far from the crease as the spot.
It is on the other side.
examples.result: $3$ cm to the right of the crease

examples.question: A rangoli has $6$ equal petals round a centre, with equal turns between them. Find its angle and order of rotational symmetry.
steps: It fits $6$ times in one full turn.

lessons.title: Rotational symmetry
lessons.introduction: Turn a figure about its centre. If it looks exactly the same before a full turn, it has rotational symmetry. The smallest such turn is the angle of symmetry. The number of matching positions in one full turn is the order. Colours count too. If the four blades of a pinwheel have four different colours, no turn less than $360^\circ$ brings every colour back to its place, so it has no rotational symmetry. Turn the pinwheel below and see.
formulas: Angle of symmetry: the smallest turn that gives the same look

items.v: same colour: turn by 90° and it looks the same · order 4

picture.caption: When all four blades have the same colour, the pinwheel looks the same after every quarter turn: order 4.

examples.question: Find the angle and order of rotational symmetry of a square.
steps: A quarter turn ($90^\circ$) gives the same look.

examples.question: Find the angle of rotational symmetry of a regular hexagon.
A shape has angle of symmetry $72^\circ$. Find its order.
A wheel has $8$ equal spokes. Find its angle and order of rotational symmetry.
steps: It fits $8$ times in one full turn.

examples.question: A shape has rotational symmetry of order $3$. Find its angle of symmetry.
A pinwheel has $4$ equal blades. Find its angle of symmetry when the blades are (a) all red (b) red, blue, red, blue (c) red, blue, green and purple.
steps: (a) A quarter turn puts a red blade on a red place.
(b) A quarter turn puts red on blue. A half turn puts red on red.
(c) Each colour comes back to its place only after a full turn.
examples.result: (a) $90^\circ$, order $4$ (b) $180^\circ$, order $2$ (c) only $360^\circ$: no rotational symmetry

lessons.title: Turning quadrilaterals
lessons.introduction: Put a quadrilateral on its outline and turn it about the point where its diagonals meet. A square fits on its outline after every quarter turn. A rectangle, a rhombus and a parallelogram fit only after a half turn. A kite and a trapezium fit only after a full turn. The simulation in this session shows this.
formulas: Kite, trapezium, isosceles trapezium: no rotational symmetry
The centre of the turn is the point where the diagonals meet

picture.caption: Lines: lines of symmetry. Diagonals: how many diagonals are lines of symmetry. Order 1 means no rotational symmetry.

examples.question: Find the angle and the order of rotational symmetry of a rectangle.
steps: After a quarter turn, the long sides stand up, so it does not fit.
After a half turn it fits.

examples.question: Does a kite have rotational symmetry?
steps: After a half turn, the short sides go to the bottom.
It fits on its outline only after a full turn.

examples.question: A parallelogram has no line of symmetry. Does it have any symmetry at all?
steps: Turn it about the point where the diagonals meet.
After a half turn it fits on its outline.

examples.question: Name a quadrilateral that has line symmetry but no rotational symmetry.
steps: A kite has $1$ line of symmetry.
It fits on its outline only after a full turn.

examples.question: Name a quadrilateral that has rotational symmetry but no line symmetry.
steps: A parallelogram (not a rectangle or a rhombus) has no line of symmetry.

lessons.title: Line symmetry and rotational symmetry together
lessons.introduction: Many shapes have both kinds of symmetry. Regular polygons have $n$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $n$. Some shapes have one kind only.
formulas: Isosceles triangle: $1$ line, no rotational symmetry

picture.caption: Lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of common shapes.

examples.question: How many lines of symmetry and what order of rotational symmetry does a rectangle have?
steps: A half turn ($180^\circ$) gives the same look: order $2$.

examples.question: Does a parallelogram (not a rectangle) have a line of symmetry?
steps: No fold makes the halves match.
But a half turn gives the same look.
examples.result: No line; rotational symmetry of order $2$

examples.question: A regular octagon has 8 equal sides. Find its lines of symmetry and its angle of symmetry.
Which has $2$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $2$: a rectangle or a rhombus?
steps: Rectangle: $2$ lines through the mid-points of opposite sides, and half-turn symmetry.
Rhombus: $2$ lines along the diagonals, and half-turn symmetry.

examples.question: Name a triangle that has line symmetry but no rotational symmetry.
steps: An isosceles triangle (not equilateral) has $1$ line.
After a turn of less than $360^\circ$ it does not fit on itself.

lessons.title: Symmetry puzzles
lessons.introduction: Look at letters, numbers and designs. Some have rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry. Designers use symmetry in rangoli, tiles and logos.

items.v: Z and N: same after a half turn
H and X: lines of symmetry and order 2

picture.caption: Z and N look the same after a half turn. H and X also have lines of symmetry.

examples.question: Which of $S$, $H$, $Z$, $E$ have rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry?
steps: $S$, $Z$: a half turn gives the same letter; no fold matches.
$H$ has lines of symmetry. $E$ has no rotational symmetry.

examples.question: Find the angle of symmetry of a regular $12$-sided figure.
A rangoli design looks the same after every $40^\circ$ turn. What is its order?
Which of $H$, $I$, $N$, $X$, $O$ have both line symmetry and rotational symmetry?
steps: $H$, $I$, $X$, $O$ have lines of symmetry and look the same after a half turn.
$N$ has a half-turn symmetry but no line of symmetry.

g6-integers.title: The Other Side of Zero
g6-integers.subtitle: Negative numbers, the number line, token models, adding and subtracting integers

sheet.title: Integers
items: Integers: $\dots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$
Positive numbers are greater than $0$; negative numbers are less than $0$
$0$ is neither positive nor negative
Opposite of $5$ is $-5$; $5+(-5)=0$

sheet.title: Order
items: On the number line, a number is greater than every number to its left
$-2>-7$ because $-2$ is to the right of $-7$
Every positive number is greater than every negative number

sheet.title: Adding and subtracting
items: Adding a positive number: move right
Adding a negative number: move left
Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite: $a-b=a+(-b)$

lessons.title: Numbers below zero
lessons.introduction: In Bela’s Building of Fun, the ground floor is 0. Floors above the ground are $+1, +2, +3$. Floors below the ground are $-1, -2, -3$. A lift button such as $-2$ means go 2 floors down.
formulas: Each positive number has an opposite negative number

picture.caption: Green floors above the ground are positive. Coral floors below the ground are negative.

examples.question: You are on floor $+2$ and press $-5$. Where does the lift stop?
You are on floor $-1$ and want to reach floor $+4$. Which button do you press?
steps: From $-1$ to $0$ is 1 floor up; from $0$ to $+4$ is 4 more.

examples.question: Write the opposite of each: $7$, $-12$, $0$.
steps: The opposite has the same size and the other sign.

lessons.title: Integers on the number line
lessons.introduction: On a number line, numbers increase from left to right. Negative numbers sit to the left of zero. A number to the right is always the greater number, even among negative numbers.
formulas: Right means greater, left means smaller
Distance from $0$ is the size of the number

picture.caption: −1 is to the right of −5, so −1 is greater than −5.

examples.question: Which is greater, $-3$ or $-8$?
steps: $-3$ is to the right of $-8$ on the number line.

examples.question: Arrange in increasing order: $2, -7, 0, -3, 5$.
steps: Read from left to right on the number line.

examples.question: How many integers lie between $-4$ and $3$?

lessons.title: The token model
lessons.introduction: Use a plus token for $+1$ and a minus token for $-1$. One plus token and one minus token together make $0$. This pair is a zero pair. Remove zero pairs to find the value of a collection.
formulas: A plus token $=+1$, a minus token $=-1$
One plus and one minus token make a zero pair: $(+1)+(-1)=0$
Value $=$ number of plus tokens $-$ number of minus tokens

picture.caption: 5 plus tokens and 3 minus tokens: 3 zero pairs cancel, so the value is +2.

examples.question: Find the value of 5 plus tokens and 3 minus tokens.
Find the value of 4 plus tokens and 9 minus tokens.
Show $-3$ with 7 tokens in all.
steps: We need (minus tokens) $-$ (plus tokens) $=3$ and (minus tokens) $+$ (plus tokens) $=7$.

lessons.title: Adding integers
lessons.introduction: To add a positive number, move to the right on the number line. To add a negative number, move to the left. With tokens, put the two collections together and remove the zero pairs.
formulas: Same signs: add the sizes, keep the sign
Different signs: subtract the sizes, keep the sign of the bigger size

picture.caption: 3 + (−5): start at 3 and move 5 steps left to −2.

examples.question: Find $3+(-5)$.
steps: Start at $3$ and move 5 steps left.

examples.question: Find $(-9)+14$.
steps: $14$ has the bigger size and it is positive.

lessons.title: Subtracting integers
lessons.introduction: Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite. To find $5-(-3)$, add the opposite of $-3$, which is $3$. With tokens, add zero pairs until you can take away the tokens you need.

picture.caption: Start with 5 plus tokens. Add 3 zero pairs. Take away the 3 minus tokens. 8 plus tokens remain: 5 − (−3) = 8.

examples.question: Find $3-7$.
steps: Different signs: $7-3=4$; the negative part is bigger.

lessons.title: Integers in daily life
lessons.introduction: Integers describe temperature below zero, money spent and money received, and heights below sea level. A deposit adds money and a withdrawal takes money away. A rise in temperature is positive and a fall is negative.

picture.caption: The temperature rises from −4 °C to 5 °C, a change of 9 degrees.

examples.question: The temperature at night was $-4^\circ$C. By noon it rose by $9^\circ$C. Find the noon temperature.
Asha has ₹250 in her account. She withdraws ₹400 using an overdraft. What is her balance?
A diver is at $-12$ m and a bird flies at $+20$ m. How far apart are they?
